Clinical Reference · Gastroenterology

Upper GI Bleed

On this page
Bleeding from a source proximal to the ligament of Treitz — presenting as hematemesis, "coffee-ground" emesis, or melena — split into non-variceal (peptic ulcer most common) and variceal (portal hypertension); the two share resuscitation but diverge sharply on drugs.
Non-variceal ≈ 80–90% PUD = #1 cause Transfuse at Hb <7 g/dL Endoscopy within 24 h Mortality ≈ 2–10% (up to 20% variceal) Anchors: IV PPI (NV) · octreotide + ceftriaxone (variceal)
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Two diseases wearing one costume

"Upper GI bleed" is a syndrome, not a diagnosis. Everything above the ligament of Treitz — esophagus, stomach, duodenum — can bleed, and the blood shows up as bright-red hematemesis, oxidised coffee-ground emesis, or, once hemoglobin is degraded by gastric acid and gut bacteria into hematin, black tarry melena. But the moment you find the source, the disease forks into two mechanistically opposite problems that demand different drugs:

  • Non-variceal (≈80–90%) — a hole in a vessel wall. Acid + pepsin (peptic ulcer disease), H. pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin, or a mechanical tear (Mallory-Weiss) erode through mucosa into an artery. The problem is a breach that a clot must plug — and gastric acid is the enemy of that clot.
  • Variceal (≈10–20%, but up to 50% of bleeds in cirrhotics) — a pressure problem. Cirrhosis raises resistance to portal flow; blood back-routes through fragile submucosal collaterals (esophageal/gastric varices) that balloon and burst under a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >12 mmHg. The problem is portal pressure, and the drugs lower it.
Non-variceal — the clot/acid axis: a platelet plug and fibrin clot only hold at pH > 6. Acid dissolves clots, activates pepsin (which digests fibrin), and impairs platelet aggregation. That single fact is why the anchor drug is a proton-pump inhibitor — raise intragastric pH above 6 and the clot on the vessel stops re-dissolving. Variceal — the portal-pressure axis: splanchnic arterial inflow feeds the varix. Octreotide/somatostatin and terlipressin constrict splanchnic arterioles → less inflow → lower portal pressure → the varix decompresses. Non-selective β-blockers do the same chronically (↓cardiac output via β1 + unopposed α splanchnic vasoconstriction via β2 blockade). Antibiotics (ceftriaxone) blunt the bacterial-translocation surge that itself worsens portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding.
Think of the gut wall as a garden hose. A non-variceal bleed is a puncture — you slap a patch (clot) over it, and your job is to keep the patch from being washed off (keep acid away → PPI). A variceal bleed is the hose over-pressurised at the spigot — the wall is thin and bulging, so you don't patch it, you turn down the water pressure (octreotide/β-blocker lower portal inflow) and then clamp the bulge (band it).
The fork: same presentation, opposite mechanisms → opposite drug anchors. Resuscitation is shared.

Classification & the Forrest ladder

Causes of upper GI bleeding (approximate share)

CauseShareKey feature
Peptic ulcer disease (gastric/duodenal)~40–50%H. pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin; risk graded by Forrest class
Esophagogastric varices~10–20%Portal hypertension; highest mortality
Erosive gastritis / esophagitis / duodenitis~10–15%NSAIDs, alcohol, stress, reflux
Mallory-Weiss tear~5–10%Retching → GE-junction laceration; usually self-limits
Angiodysplasia / GAVE ("watermelon stomach")~5%Vascular ectasia; oozing, often recurrent, iron-deficiency
Malignancy (gastric/esophageal)~3–5%Weight loss, chronic anemia
Dieulafoy lesion~1–2%Aberrant large submucosal artery; brisk, hard to find
Aortoenteric fistula<1%Prior aortic graft; "herald bleed" then exsanguination

Forrest classification of peptic-ulcer stigmata → rebleeding risk & who needs endoscopic therapy

ForrestStigma of hemorrhageRebleed risk (untreated)Endoscopic therapy?
IaActive spurting (arterial)~55–90%Yes — always
IbActive oozing~10–27%Yes
IIaNon-bleeding visible vessel~50%Yes
IIbAdherent clot~22–33%Consider (irrigate ± treat underlying vessel)
IIcFlat pigmented spot~7–10%No — PPI alone
IIIClean ulcer base~3–5%No — PPI alone, feed early
The Forrest class is the single most useful thing your GI colleague tells you post-scope: Ia/Ib/IIa/IIb = "high-risk stigmata" → endoscopic hemostasis + 72 h of IV PPI and inpatient observation; IIc/III = low-risk → oral PPI, early feeding, and often early discharge.
📊

Presentation — signs, frequency & why they happen

Sign / symptom~FreqWhy it happens
Melena (black, tarry, malodorous stool)~70%Hemoglobin oxidised to hematin by gastric acid + gut bacteria; needs as little as 50 mL blood and ~14 h transit. Signals an upper source ~90% of the time.
Hematemesis (bright red or coffee-ground)~50%Blood refluxed/vomited from esophagus, stomach, or duodenum; coffee-ground = partially digested by acid (slower/older bleed).
Fatigue / dyspnea / lightheadedness~40–60%Anemia + reduced oxygen-carrying capacity; orthostatic cerebral hypoperfusion.
Epigastric pain / dyspepsia~30–40%Underlying peptic ulcer / gastritis; pain may paradoxically improve as blood buffers acid.
Tachycardia (HR >100)~30%Compensatory sympathetic response to hypovolemia — often the earliest vital-sign change.
Orthostatic hypotension / syncope~15–30%≥15% blood-volume loss; syncope implies a large, brisk bleed.
Hematochezia (from an upper source)~10–15%Massive UGIB with rapid transit — blood is cathartic; implies >1 L loss and is a bad sign (unstable).
Frank shock (SBP <90, cool, oliguric)~10%≥30–40% blood-volume loss; the marker for ICU-level care.
Stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider angiomata, ascites, caput medusae)~10–15%Point to a variceal source — change your empiric drugs before the scope.
An elevated BUN:creatinine ratio (>20–30:1) with normal kidneys is a classic tell of UGIB: intestinal bacteria digest the hemoglobin protein load into urea (a "GI protein meal"), while volume depletion adds a pre-renal component. It also drives points on the Glasgow-Blatchford score.
🔬

Reading the labs — why each value moves (and the traps)

LabDirection in UGIBMechanismConfounder / false reading
Hemoglobin / hematocrit↓ (but delayed)Loss of red-cell massFalsely normal early — whole blood is lost, so the Hb concentration doesn't fall until plasma re-equilibrates (hours) or you give crystalloid (dilutes). A "normal" Hb never rules out an acute bleed.
BUN↑Intestinal bacteria digest the hemoglobin protein load → urea; plus pre-renal volume depletionAlso rises in dehydration, steroids, high-protein feeds; the tell is a disproportionate BUN vs creatinine. Falsely low in liver failure (can't make urea).
BUN:Cr ratio↑ (>20–30:1)Combination of enteric protein load + pre-renal stateBlunted if there is intrinsic renal disease raising creatinine. A high ratio supports (doesn't prove) an upper source.
MCV↓ (if chronic)Iron deficiency from chronic occult lossNormal/high MCV in acute bleeding or with concurrent B₁₂/folate deficiency or alcohol use.
Platelets↓ (variable)Consumption in massive bleed; splenic sequestration in cirrhosisCirrhotics are baseline thrombocytopenic; count doesn't reflect the qualitative platelet defect in uremia (normal count, poor function).
INR↑ (variable)Dilution, consumption, or underlying liver disease/warfarinA modestly high INR (≤2.5) does not preclude endoscopic hemostasis — don't delay the scope to chase it.
Lactate↑Hypoperfusion from hypovolemiaAlso rises with metformin, seizures, regional ischemia; trend it as a resuscitation marker.
LFTs / albuminAbnormal → cirrhosisScreens for the portal-hypertension pathwayAlbumin falls in acute illness generally; low albumin also scores AIMS65.

Reading the endoscopy report (what the words mean for you)

Endoscopic findingWhat it tells youAction it triggers
Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa (spurting, oozing, visible vessel)High-risk stigmata → high rebleedingEndoscopic hemostasis (clip/thermal, never epi alone) + 72 h IV PPI; admit/monitor
Forrest IIb (adherent clot)Intermediate; may hide a vesselConsider clot removal ± treat underlying vessel; high-dose PPI
Forrest IIc/III (flat spot / clean base)Low rebleeding riskOral PPI, early feeding, early discharge candidate
Varices with red wale marks / white nippleRecent or high-risk-of-bleeding varixBand ligation (or glue for gastric fundal) + variceal bundle
Gastric ulcerCould be malignantBiopsy + repeat EGD in 8–12 wk to confirm healing

Where each drug acts

Every drug in this guide maps to one of these two columns. Keep the column in mind and the dosing makes sense.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient triage, prevention & secondary prophylaxis
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Outpatient presentation & who is at risk

Most true UGIB presents to the ED, but the clinic sees the milder and the recovering end of the spectrum: intermittent melena, iron-deficiency anemia of unclear source, coffee-ground emesis in someone who feels "fine," or a cirrhotic due for variceal surveillance. Your clinic job is three-fold — decide who is safe to scope as an outpatient vs send to the ED, prevent the first (or next) bleed, and run secondary prophylaxis.

Highest-risk histories: NSAID/aspirin use, prior peptic ulcer or H. pylori, known cirrhosis/varices, anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy, chronic kidney disease (uremic platelet dysfunction), heavy alcohol use, and prior aortic graft (aortoenteric fistula "herald bleed").

A single episode of hematemesis, syncope, ongoing melena, orthostatic vitals, or resting tachycardia is not an outpatient problem — direct to the ED. See the presentation-frequency table in Pathophysiology for how these track with blood-volume loss.

Treat

Prevention & secondary prophylaxis

💊

Non-variceal: heal the ulcer, kill the cause

1
Acid suppression — PPI
Heal the ulcer, prevent recurrence.
▾
PPIs irreversibly block the parietal-cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase → intragastric pH >4 for healing (and >6 for clot stability during a bleed). All PPIs are roughly equivalent at standard doses; choose by cost/availability and drug interactions.
DrugStartTitration → targetWhy / notesIf intolerant
Omeprazole20–40 mg PO dailyUncomplicated ulcer 4–8 wk; if high-risk endoscopic ulcer, BID → daily. Gastric ulcer: repeat EGD to confirm healing/exclude cancer.Prototype PPI; inhibits CYP2C19 (↓ clopidogrel activation — prefer pantoprazole with clopidogrel).Pantoprazole / rabeprazole
Pantoprazole40 mg PO daily40 mg daily–BID × 4–8 wkLeast CYP2C19 interaction → best with clopidogrel.Esomeprazole
Esomeprazole20–40 mg PO daily40 mg daily × 4–8 wkS-isomer of omeprazole; potent.Lansoprazole
H₂-blocker (famotidine)20–40 mg PO BIDOnly if PPI truly not toleratedWeaker/tachyphylaxis; NOT adequate for high-risk ulcer.— (PPI strongly preferred)
Monitor on chronic PPI: long-term risks (B₁₂/iron/magnesium deficiency, ↑ C. difficile/pneumonia, possible fracture) — use the lowest effective dose and de-prescribe once the cause is fixed. Don't reflexively continue lifelong PPI after H. pylori eradication + NSAID cessation.
2
Eradicate H. pylori
The single biggest driver of rebleeding — treat & confirm.
▾
RegimenComponentsDurationWhen to pickIf penicillin-allergic
Bismuth quadruplePPI BID + bismuth subsalicylate QID + tetracycline QID + metronidazole TID–QID14 daysPreferred first-line (esp. prior macrolide exposure or high clarithromycin resistance).Penicillin-free — safe in allergy
Clarithromycin triplePPI BID + amoxicillin + clarithromycin14 daysOnly where clarithromycin resistance <15% and no prior macrolide.Use bismuth quadruple instead
Always confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after therapy and ≥2 weeks off PPI (urea breath test or stool antigen). Eradication drops ulcer rebleeding from ~20% to a few percent.
3
Manage NSAID / aspirin / anticoagulant risk
Remove or protect against the injurious drug.
▾
  • NSAIDs: stop if non-essential. If required, lowest dose + co-prescribe PPI, or switch to a COX-2 selective (celecoxib) + PPI in high-risk patients.
  • Aspirin for secondary CV prevention: do not permanently stop — resume low-dose aspirin early (within ~3–7 days once hemostasis secured) with PPI cover; withholding it raises cardiovascular death more than it prevents rebleeding (Sung 2010).
  • Anticoagulation: individualize restart (usually within days once hemostasis secure); shortest interruption for mechanical valves.
🩸

Variceal: secondary prophylaxis (after an index variceal bleed)

First-line secondary prophylaxis (Baveno VII) = NSBB + endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL). NSBBs lower portal pressure (β1 ↓ cardiac output + β2 block → unopposed α splanchnic vasoconstriction; carvedilol adds α1 blockade → ↓ intrahepatic resistance). EVL obliterates the varices mechanically. Combining beats either alone.
DrugStartTitration → target/maxWhy / titrate toIf intolerant
Carvedilol (preferred)6.25 mg PO daily (or 3.125 mg BID)↑ to 12.5 mg/day as tolerated; keep SBP >90–100Baveno VII first choice; dosed to blood pressure, not heart rate; strongest portal-pressure drop.Propranolol or nadolol
Propranolol20–40 mg PO BIDDouble ~q2–3 days to max tolerated; target resting HR 55–60; max ~320 mg/dayNon-selective β-blocker; titrate to HR, keep SBP ≥90.Nadolol (once-daily)
Nadolol20–40 mg PO daily↑ to max tolerated; target HR 55–60Once-daily, renally cleared; good adherence.Carvedilol
EVLBanding sessionRepeat q1–4 weeks until varices eradicated, then surveillance EGDMechanical obliteration of the varix.TIPS if refractory rebleeding
Hold NSBBs during acute variceal bleeding / hypotension (they blunt the compensatory tachycardia and drop BP) — they are a prophylaxis drug, resumed once stable, never an acute-bleed drug.
Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Gastric ulcer: repeat EGD in 8–12 weeks to confirm healing and exclude malignancy (duodenal ulcers generally don't need repeat scope).
  • H. pylori: confirm eradication ≥4 wk post-therapy, off PPI ≥2 wk.
  • Anemia: recheck CBC ~2–4 weeks after discharge; replete iron.
  • Varices (cirrhosis): surveillance EGD per Baveno; up-titrate NSBB to target HR/BP at each visit; band until eradicated.
  • Chronic PPI: reassess need annually; check magnesium if on long-term therapy with symptoms.
Prevent

USPSTF & prevention

🛡️

Relevant USPSTF recommendations

GradeRecommendationPopulation / relevance to UGIB
C / DAspirin for primary CVD prevention (2022): individualize ages 40–59 at ≥10% 10-yr risk (Grade C); do NOT initiate at ≥60 (Grade D)GI bleeding risk is the central reason the USPSTF pulled back — a direct UGIB-prevention lever in clinic.
BScreen for hepatitis C (all adults 18–79) & hepatitis B (high-risk) → identify/treat before cirrhosisPrevents the portal-hypertension pathway to variceal bleeding.
BUnhealthy alcohol-use screening & brief intervention (adults ≥18)Alcohol drives both gastritis/PUD and cirrhosis/varices.

Note: there is no USPSTF general-population H. pylori screening recommendation — test-and-treat is disease-driven (dyspepsia, PUD, MALT).

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED immediately for: hematemesis (especially red blood), hematochezia with any instability, syncope/presyncope or orthostatic vitals, resting tachycardia, ongoing melena, GBS ≥2, known cirrhosis/varices, anticoagulation, or significant anemia/comorbidity.
The outpatient-endoscopy pathway is only for the GBS ≤1, hemodynamically normal patient with reliable follow-up. When in doubt, they cross the street to the ED.
🛏️ Wards — resuscitate, risk-stratify, scope within 24 h
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Admit essentially any UGIB that is not GBS ≤1: hemodynamic change, active/ongoing bleeding, significant anemia or transfusion need, cirrhosis/varices, anticoagulation, or major comorbidity. The first 30 minutes are ABC + two large-bore IVs + resuscitate, then risk-stratify and decide floor vs ICU.

The very first fork at the bedside: does this look variceal? Known cirrhosis, stigmata of liver disease, or ascites → start the variceal bundle (octreotide + ceftriaxone) empirically before the scope, while still doing the shared resuscitation. If clearly non-variceal → IV PPI pathway.

Score

AIMS65 — mortality risk

🧮

AIMS65 — 5-factor in-hospital mortality predictor

Fast, uses only admission data. Each factor = 1 point (range 0–5). Rising score → rising mortality and need for ICU/transfusion.

Albumin <3.0 g/dL +1
INR >1.5 +1
Altered Mental status (GCS <14) +1
Systolic BP ≤90 mmHg +1
Age ≥65 years +1
0
Mortality bands (validation): 0 ≈ 0.3% · 1 ≈ 1% · 2 ≈ 3% · 3 ≈ 9% · 4 ≈ 15% · 5 ≈ 25% (AIMS65 validation, AJG 2015). Score ≥2 flags a patient who probably belongs on monitored/step-down care. For post-endoscopic rebleeding/mortality use the full Rockall score (MDCalc).
Treat

Acute management

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy

1
Resuscitate + restrictive transfusion
Shared across variceal & non-variceal.
▾
Restrictive transfusion (transfuse at Hb <7 g/dL, target 7–9) improved 6-week survival (95% vs 91%) and reduced rebleeding vs a liberal Hb <9 strategy — over-transfusion raises portal pressure and pops variceal clots (Villanueva 2013 NEJM; ACG 2021 strong rec).
  • RBC: transfuse at Hb <7 (target 7–9). Use a higher threshold (~<8) in ACS/active ischemia, or transfuse to clinical response in massive ongoing hemorrhage.
  • Platelets: if <50×10⁹/L with active bleeding.
  • Coagulopathy: correct clinically significant coagulopathy but do not delay endoscopy to fully normalize a modestly elevated INR (≤2.5 does not preclude hemostasis).
  • Tranexamic acid: do NOT use (HALT-IT 2020 — no benefit, more VTE/seizures).
2A
Non-variceal pathway — IV PPI + endoscopy
Peptic ulcer / erosive disease.
▾
DrugStartTitration / durationWhy it worksAlt / notes
Pantoprazole (IV)80 mg IV bolus, then 8 mg/hr infusionContinue ×72 h after endoscopic therapy of high-risk stigmata (Ia/Ib/IIa)pH >6 stabilizes clot; ↓ rebleeding 22.5%→6.7% (Lau 2000).Esomeprazole same regimen
PPI — intermittent (alt)80 mg IV/PO, then 40 mg q12h×72 h — non-inferior to infusion (meta-analysis 2014)Same clot-stabilizing effect; simpler/cheaper.Preferred if no pump available
Erythromycin (prokinetic)250 mg IV (3 mg/kg)Once, 30–90 min before endoscopyMotilin agonist empties gastric blood → better view, fewer repeat scopes.Check QT; avoid if prolonged
Endoscopy within 24 h of presentation after resuscitation (ACG 2021). Urgent (<6 h) endoscopy does not improve mortality over early (Lau 2020 NEJM) — resuscitate first. High-risk stigmata get endoscopic hemostasis (clip or thermal; epinephrine injection never alone) + 72 h IV PPI; low-risk (IIc/III) get oral PPI and early feeding.
After the 72-h infusion, step down to oral PPI BID through day 14 for endoscopically-treated high-risk ulcers, then once daily × 4–8 weeks (ACG 2021).
2B
Variceal pathway — the bundle (start on suspicion)
Vasoactive + antibiotic + EVL.
▾
Three interventions, each with a survival or rebleeding benefit — start the drug + antibiotic before the scope whenever variceal bleeding is suspected.
DrugStartDuration / titrationWhy it worksAlt
Octreotide50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/hr infusionContinue ×3–5 daysSomatostatin analog → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal inflow/pressure.Somatostatin 250 mcg bolus → 250 mcg/hr
Terlipressin2 mg IV q4h until controlThen 1 mg q4h; the only vasoactive with a mortality benefitVasopressin V1 analog → direct splanchnic vasoconstriction.Watch hyponatremia/ischemia; use octreotide if unavailable

3
Rebleeding / refractory
Repeat scope, IR, or TIPS.
▾
  • Non-variceal rebleed: repeat endoscopy (don't routinely do "second-look"; repeat only on rebleed) → if fails, IR transcatheter arterial embolization → surgery last.
  • Variceal rebleed / high-risk: early/pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h (Child C ≤13, or Child B with active bleeding) improves survival (García-Pagán 2010); salvage TIPS for any refractory variceal bleed.

Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change the course & the management

ComorbidityEffect on the bleedWhat it changes
Cirrhosis / portal HTNAssume variceal; coagulopathy + thrombocytopenia; encephalopathy from blood loadEmpiric octreotide + ceftriaxone before scope; restrictive transfusion is critical; early TIPS by Child class; lactulose
CKD / uremiaUremic platelet dysfunction (normal count, poor function) → prolonged bleedingDDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV over 15–30 min (releases vWF; tachyphylaxis after ~2 doses); dialysis; keep Hb ~10
CAD on DAPT / recent stentStopping antiplatelets risks stent thrombosisContinue aspirin if possible; resume P2Y12 ASAP after hemostasis (cardiology); do not reflexively transfuse platelets
Anticoagulation (AF, VTE, valve)Amplifies bleeding; reversal needed for life-threatening bleedReverse per agent (see ICU); mechanical valve = shortest interruption; restart within days once hemostasis secure
ACS / active ischemiaAnemia worsens myocardial oxygen supplyHigher transfusion threshold (~Hb <8); balance antiplatelet needs
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in acute UGIB: tranexamic acid (HALT-IT harm signal); routine NG lavage; routine platelet transfusion for antiplatelet reversal; NSAIDs; over-/liberal transfusion; delaying endoscopy to fully normalize a mildly elevated INR; and NSBBs during active variceal bleeding/hypotension (hold, then resume for prophylaxis).
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Serial hemoglobin q6–12h while active; a falling Hb off transfusion = rebleeding until proven otherwise.
  • Vitals + orthostatics, urine output, lactate — perfusion trend.
  • Signs of rebleeding: fresh hematemesis/melena, new tachycardia, Hb drop.
  • Mental status (encephalopathy in cirrhotics), and response to lactulose.
  • Diet: feed early after low-risk endoscopy; advance as tolerated.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers (numeric)

Transfer to ICU for: SBP <90 or shock index >1 despite resuscitation; ongoing/massive bleeding or transfusion of ≥2–4 units in the first hours / continuing requirement; active hematemesis with airway/aspiration risk or altered mental status (intubate); variceal bleeding with instability; need for vasoactive/vasopressor support, balloon tamponade, or TIPS; or significant comorbidity with poor reserve.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: hemostasis achieved (low-risk stigmata or successfully treated), hemodynamically stable, stable Hb without ongoing transfusion (typically ~24–48 h of stability for high-risk ulcers), tolerating diet/oral meds, PPI + H. pylori/NSAID plan set, anticoagulation/antiplatelet plan documented, and follow-up (repeat EGD for gastric ulcers) arranged.

Home

Stable, low-risk stigmata, reliable, can take oral PPI & follow up.

Home health

Home + nursing for iron infusions, INR checks, or frailty support.

SNF

Deconditioned/elderly needing 24h skilled nursing, <3h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rare — significant deconditioning able to tolerate ≥3h therapy/day.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (e.g., ventilator/critical-illness recovery).

Hospice / palliative

Bleeding malignancy or end-stage cirrhosis with goals-of-care shift.
🫀 ICU — massive hemorrhage, reversal & rescue
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

UGIB reaches the ICU when the bleed outpaces resuscitation or the airway is threatened:

  • Hemodynamic instability — SBP <90, shock index (HR/SBP) >1, or shock despite volume + blood.
  • Massive hematemesis or ongoing transfusion requirement.
  • Variceal hemorrhage in decompensated cirrhosis (Child B/C).
  • Altered mental status / airway risk — aspiration danger during active hematemesis.
  • Need for balloon tamponade, TIPS, IR embolization, or vasopressors.
Monitor

Access, monitoring & MTP

🩸

Lines, transfusion strategy, targets

  • Access: two large-bore peripheral IVs (14–16 g, flow beats a triple-lumen central line) ± central venous access for pressors; arterial line for continuous BP.
  • Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) for uncontrolled hemorrhage: balanced resuscitation approximating RBC:FFP:platelets ≈ 1:1:1; use TEG/ROTEM to guide where available.
  • Watch the "lethal triad" (acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy): monitor ionized calcium (citrate → hypocalcemia — replace), potassium, and temperature (warm fluids).
  • Once controlled, revert to the restrictive Hb <7 target; during active massive bleeding, transfuse to clinical response rather than a number.

Reverse

Anticoagulation reversal & support

💉

Which agent reverses which drug — with doses

AnticoagulantReversal agent / mechanismDoseNotes
Warfarin (VKA)Vitamin K + 4-factor PCC (Kcentra) — replaces II, VII, IX, XVitamin K 10 mg IV (slow) + 4F-PCC 25–50 units/kg by INR (or fixed ~1500 units for non-ICH major bleed)FFP only if PCC unavailable; PCC is faster and lower-volume.
Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor)Idarucizumab (Praxbind) — monoclonal Fab binds dabigatran5 g IV (two 2.5 g boluses ≤15 min apart)Dialysis also removes dabigatran (RE-VERSE AD).
Apixaban / rivaroxaban (factor Xa inhibitors)Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) — decoy factor Xa; or 4F-PCCLow: 400 mg bolus + 4 mg/min ×120 min; High: 800 mg bolus + 8 mg/min ×120 min. If unavailable → 4F-PCC 50 units/kgDose by agent, amount, and time since last dose.
Heparin (UFH)Protamine sulfate — binds/neutralizes heparin1 mg per 100 units heparin (max 50 mg)LMWH only partially reversed by protamine.
Antiplatelet (ASA/clopidogrel)Hold drug; platelets generally NOT helpful (may harm in ICH)Consider DDAVP case-by-caseWeigh cardiac/stent-thrombosis risk of stopping.
Uremic platelet dysfunctionDDAVP — releases endothelial vWF/factor VIII0.3 mcg/kg IV over 15–30 minOnset ~1 h; tachyphylaxis after ~2 doses.
For persistent shock despite adequate volume and blood, norepinephrine (0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min, α1>β1 → ↑SVR) is the first-line pressor as a bridge to hemostasis — but blood, not pressors, is the treatment for hemorrhagic shock.
Airway

Airway protection

🌬️

When to intubate for a GI bleed

Intubate for airway protection before endoscopy in massive hematemesis, altered mental status/encephalopathy, or high aspiration risk — a controlled airway prevents aspiration and lets endoscopy proceed safely. Extubate after hemostasis when the patient is protecting the airway.

Indication
Airway protection
massive hematemesis / ↓GCS
Mode
AC/VC
post-intubation default
Tidal volume
6–8 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective
Aspiration risk
RSI + suction
stomach full of blood
The stomach is full of blood — treat every intubation as a full-stomach rapid-sequence induction with good suction ready. Post-hemostasis, these patients often extubate quickly.
Rescue

Advanced / mechanical rescue

⚙️

Refractory-bleeding algorithms

A
Balloon tamponade (variceal bridge)
Sengstaken-Blakemore / Minnesota tube.
▾

For uncontrolled/exsanguinating esophageal variceal bleeding refractory to drugs + endoscopy, as a temporizing bridge (≤24 h) to TIPS/repeat EVL. Requires endotracheal intubation first. Immediate hemostasis 50–90%, but ~50% rebleed on deflation and complication rate ~14% (esophageal rupture, aspiration, mucosal necrosis, asphyxiation from migration). Confirm gastric-balloon position on radiograph before full inflation. Covered self-expanding metal esophageal stents are an increasingly used, lower-complication alternative.

B
Early / pre-emptive TIPS (variceal)
Definitive portal decompression.
▾
A PTFE-covered shunt from portal to hepatic vein drops portal pressure directly. In Child C (≤13) or Child B with active bleeding at endoscopy, placing TIPS within 72 h (ideally <24 h) cut rebleeding (1-yr freedom 93% vs 50%) and improved 1-year survival (86% vs 61%) — García-Pagán 2010 NEJM. Salvage TIPS for any refractory variceal bleed. Watch for post-TIPS encephalopathy.
C
IR embolization / surgery (non-variceal)
When endoscopy fails.
▾

Transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) is first-line rescue for non-variceal bleeding refractory to endoscopy (e.g., gastroduodenal-artery embolization for a posterior duodenal ulcer). CT angiography can localize active bleeding (needs ~0.3–0.5 mL/min) before angiography. Surgery is the last resort when IR and endoscopy fail.

Sengstaken-Blakemore tube — gastric + esophageal balloons tamponade varices as a ≤24 h bridge (intubate first).

Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: hemostasis achieved, hemodynamically stable off vasopressors, no ongoing transfusion requirement, stable serial Hb (no drop over ~12–24 h), extubated and protecting the airway, and a resolving lactate.
Not yet if: still needing blood to hold Hb, any fresh hematemesis/melena, borderline pressures, or a high-risk variceal patient within the first 24–48 h of a TIPS/tamponade rescue.

Sources, trials & credits

Landmark trials

Trial (year)QuestionResultWhy it matters
Villanueva (2013, NEJM)Restrictive (Hb <7) vs liberal (<9) transfusion, 921 severe UGIBRestrictive → better 6-wk survival (95% vs 91%, HR 0.55), less rebleedingBasis for the Hb <7 transfusion threshold
García-Pagán (2010, NEJM)Early PTFE-covered TIPS <72 h vs drug+endoscopy in high-risk cirrhotics↓ rebleeding (1-yr free 93% vs 50%), ↑ 1-yr survival (86% vs 61%)Basis for early/pre-emptive TIPS
Lau (2000, NEJM)High-dose IV omeprazole vs placebo after endoscopic therapyRebleeding 6.7% vs 22.5%Basis for high-dose PPI after hemostasis
Lau (2020, NEJM)Urgent (<6 h) vs early (6–24 h) endoscopy in high-risk UGIBNo mortality difference (8.9% vs 6.6%)Endoscopy within 24 h — faster is not better; resuscitate first
Sung (2010, Ann Intern Med)Continue vs stop aspirin after ulcer bleedContinuing: slightly ↑ rebleed but markedly ↓ all-cause/CV mortalityResume aspirin early in secondary-prevention patients
HALT-IT (2020, Lancet)Tranexamic acid vs placebo, 12,009 GI-bleed patientsNo mortality benefit; ↑ VTE and seizuresDo NOT use TXA for GI bleeding
TRIGGER (2015, Lancet)Cluster feasibility trial, restrictive vs liberal transfusionFeasible; supported restrictive adoptionReinforced the restrictive strategy
Baveno VII (2022)International portal-hypertension consensusCarvedilol preferred NSBB; vasoactive 2–5 d + antibiotics + EVL; early TIPS in high-riskFramework for all variceal management
